name: Rye quick-start
tagline: The fastest, most forgiving start. Whole rye carries the most microbes and food.
why: Every flour test we found put rye first for speed, and the science explains why: rye and other high-bran flours bring more minerals, more sugars and more microbes. This is the starter most likely to work first time.

schedule.step: Stir 50 g whole rye and 50 g water into a thick paste in a clean straight-sided jar. Mark the level with a rubber band. Cover loosely and keep at 24 to 26 °C.
Once a day: keep 25 g, discard the rest, and feed 50 g rye and 50 g water (1:2:2). A big rise on day 2 is bacteria, not yeast; a quiet day 3 or 4 is normal. Don't feed more often yet.

schedule.when: From the first clear rise after day 4
schedule.step: Feed twice a day, 07:00 and 19:00: keep 20 g, add 40 g rye and 40 g water (1:2:2).
It at least doubles within 6 to 8 hours of a feed, three feeds in a row, and smells sour and fruity, not of nail polish or old cheese.
Keep it in the fridge and feed once a week at 1:2:2. To bake, take it out the night before and give it one or two feeds at room temperature.

journal: Rye is thick, so it rises less than a wheat starter. Compare it against itself from feed to feed, not against B and C.

name: Juice start, whole wheat
tagline: Skips the false rise by starting acidic, following a microbiologist's method.
expected: Yeast by day 3 to 5, ready in about 10 to 14 days
why: Most new starters are taken over in the first days by gassy flour bacteria that give a false rise and odd smells. Starting with unsweetened pineapple juice makes the mix acidic from day one, so those bacteria never get going and the real sourdough microbes arrive sooner.

schedule.step: Mix 15 g whole wheat flour and 30 g unsweetened pineapple juice (100% juice, from a carton is fine). Cover loosely, keep at 24 to 26 °C, and stir once in the morning.
Add 15 g whole wheat and 30 g juice. Don't discard. Stir well.
Switch to water. Once a day: keep 55 g, discard the rest, and feed 28 g whole wheat and 28 g water. Carry on until it clearly expands and smells yeasty.
Feed twice a day, 07:00 and 19:00, on half-white flour: keep 20 g, add 40 g Halbweissmehl and 40 g water (1:2:2).
It at least doubles within 6 to 8 hours of a feed, three feeds in a row, with a pleasant yoghurt-like tang.
If nothing happens for three days after day 4, skip one feed to let the acid build, then use whole wheat for a couple of feeds.

journal: Note the day the first real rise appears. Compare it with A and C: if the juice works, B should skip the day-2 burst.

name: Half and half, slow and steady
tagline: The everyday baker's starter. Mild, lively, and built to fit a working week.
why: A blend of whole grain and white is what most professional bakers keep, and in a side-by-side test it made the best-tasting loaf. The feeds start small and step up as the starter gets stronger, the way the research suggests, so it ends on a 1:5:5 ratio that peaks about 12 hours later: one feed before work, bake-ready by evening.

schedule.step: Mix the two flours with the water. Cover loosely and leave for 48 hours at 24 to 26 °C. Stir once a day.
Once a day: keep 20 g, discard the rest, and feed 20 g flour mix and 20 g water (1:1:1).
Twice a day, 07:00 and 19:00, still at 1:1:1.
Step up to 1:2:2: keep 20 g, feed 40 g flour mix and 40 g water, twice a day.

schedule.when: When it doubles within 8 hours at 1:2:2
schedule.step: It is ready. Try 1:5:5 (10 g starter, 50 g flour mix, 50 g water). It should peak in about 10 to 12 hours, which is the routine to keep.
Fridge, fed once a week. Two room-temperature feeds before a bake day.

journal: Note the date each step-up becomes possible. That is how you will see C getting stronger.
